A mutex, short for "mutual exclusion," is a synchronization primitive that guards a critical section, meaning a stretch of code that touches shared data and must not run in more than one thread at once. A thread acquires (locks) the mutex before entering that section and releases it on the way out. Only one thread can hold the mutex at a time. Any other thread that tries to acquire it waits until it is released, so updates to shared state can't interleave and corrupt each other.

Mutexes are easy to misuse. If two threads each hold one lock while waiting for the other's, neither can make progress, and the program freezes in a deadlock. The usual defenses are to acquire locks in a consistent order and to hold them as briefly as possible.

Locking happens constantly in concurrent code, so its cost adds up. On Linux, mutexes are built on the futex ("fast userspace mutex"). When a lock is uncontended, the futex acquires and releases it entirely in user space with atomic operations. It makes a system call into the kernel only when a thread has to sleep or be woken.
